newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - BSkyB, OzEmail in Internet advert venture.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - BSkyB, OzEmail in Internet advert venture.

text.p: British Sky Broadcasting, the satellite television company controlled by Rupert Murdoch and an Australian Internet service company on Wednesday said they formed a joint venture designed to harness the vast, global advertising potential of the Internet.

BSkyB and Sydney-based OzEmail Ltd said they will invest equally in the joint venture, which is designed to capitalise on the thousands of World Wide Web sites on the Internet, an international network of computer databases.

The companies said the venture will be based on technology developed by OzEmail and will deliver advertising targeted at local audiences on Web sites throughout the world, regardless of where the Web site is hosted.

"From its inception, BSkyB has been at the cutting edge of communications technology," BSkyB chief executive Sam Chisholm said in a statement. "We are delighted to be associated with OzEmail in this venture, which we regard as one of the world's most innovative and aggressive Internet companies."

"With global Internet advertising revenue expected to exceed $5 billion by the turn of the century, this new medium represents both a sizeable and an exciting opportunity," OzEmail chairman Malcolm Turnbull said in a statement.

Turnbull and Elisabeth Murdoch, general manager of broadcasting for BSkyB, were named co-chairmen of the new joint venture. The two companies said details of the joint venture's technology and its strategy will be announced at the venture's launch on December 3 in New York.
Officials of the two companies were not available for comment.
But advertising executives involved in the Internet and new media opportunities and analysts said the venture is an attempt to bring order to a huge, but chaotic marketplace.
"Internet advertising revenue is this great pot of gold out there," Deborah Monas, a multimedia analyst with Kagan World Media in England, told Reuters in a phone interview.
Advertising, she said, "is the only way out there to make money off the Internet. Unfortunately, it's not working yet."
Monas said she expects that the joint venture will form a link between BSkyB's huge market in digital television and the Internet.

BSkyB, whose television interests stretch from Britain and across Europe to Asia, has previously said that it plans to offer access to the Internet via conventional television sets when it launches its digital service in Britain in 1997.
"I think the Internet is going to be a big part of digital television services," Monas said. "They're going to use that satellite beam as a way of getting onto the Internet."

One of the great frustrations for current users of the Internet is the slowness of the current telecommunications links, making it difficult to log onto Web sites at certain times of day and making it very time-consuming to download some sites -- particularly those with elaborate graphics.
"Satellite gives you much more bandwidth than a telephone," said Monas. "You don't have to wait 10 minutes. You can have moving pictures and music."

Estimates of current advertising revenues generated on the Internet vary greatly, and advertising professionals said there has yet to be any sound tracking method developed. But one advertising executive noted that worldwide spending on advertising in 1996 -- across all media -- totalled $290 billion. Advertising on the Internet remains a very small piece of the total pie, with many seeing it as only one percent of the total market.
If global advertising revenues rise to $350 billion in the year 2000, at one percent Internet advertising would reach $3 billion.

Some companies are already making money off advertising on the Internet, but Monas said most is being made by the browsers, such as Yahoo! Inc and Hot Wired, which offer indexes to Web sites on the Internet.
"The browsers make a lot of money off advertising," Monas said.
But although the Internet is attracting tens of millions of users, the amorphous nature of the medium makes it difficult to use for advertising.

Charles Fallon, managing consultant for Saatchi & Saatchi Vision, a unit of advertising and marketing group Cordiant Plc, said that unlike other media such as television and magazines which are aimed at people and built around certain areas of interest, Web sites on the Internet are built around companies.
"If you go into W H Smith and look at the magazine, it's grouped around areas of interest," Fallon said. "If you go into the Internet it isn't."
"Whoever develops the best navigation sites based on the consumer will win the battle" on the Internet, he said.
Fallon said the BSkyB-OzEmail joint venture might take advantage of the Internet by targeting information to particular users.
In addition, viewing advertising on a Web site requires an active decision by the user, who must click on a spot on the computer screen to bring up an advert."
"That is the big problem," said Kagan's Monas. "Internet advertising doesn't have a captive market."
